opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons, and they stack on top of each other.

The first is just the nature of what we do. We work on evaluations for things like scheming and deceptive alignment, so we often get early or privileged access to frontier models, sometimes before they're released and sometimes with more visibility than the public gets. If labs are going to trust us with that, we have to be at least as careful as they are, ideally more so. If an external evaluator becomes the weak link, the leak through which model weights, internal details, or unreleased capabilities get out, that's bad for the world and it destroys the whole third-party evaluation ecosystem. Labs would reasonably say, "why would we give anyone access again?"

The second reason is about the content of our own work. Some of what we build is somewhat sensitive. If you're developing evals that test whether a model can evade oversight, or you're cataloguing the specific ways models behave deceptively, some of that is useful for people who want to make models better at exactly those things. And if our eval sets leak into training data, they stop measuring what they're supposed to measure. A contaminated benchmark is worse than useless because it gives you false confidence.

The third reason is more forward-looking. Right now the stakes are moderate. But if things go the way many of us expect, the models we're evaluating will become much more capable, and the information around them, weights, capability profiles, specific vulnerabilities, becomes a target for well-resourced actors, including state-level ones. Good security culture can't be built overnight when you suddenly need it. It's habits, processes, who you hire, how you handle access. So we'd rather build it while we're small and it's relatively cheap than retrofit it later.

And finally, there's a credibility point. We're asking AI developers to take risks seriously and to behave responsibly under uncertainty. It would be a bit hypocritical if we didn't hold ourselves to a high standard on the things within our own control. Security is one of the clearest places where we can actually walk the talk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different angles on this, and it took us a little while to appreciate how much it matters.

The most obvious one is that we work with frontier models and frontier labs. When we do pre-deployment evaluations, we often get access to models before they're released, sometimes with fewer safeguards, sometimes with information about how they were trained or what capabilities the lab is worried about. That's extremely sensitive. If a lab is going to trust you with that, they need to believe you won't leak it, whether through carelessness or because someone actively targets you. So in a very practical sense, security is the price of admission. If we can't demonstrate it, we don't get access, and if we don't get access, we can't do the work we think is most important.

The second angle is about the research itself. A lot of what we do is on scheming and deceptive alignment, and part of that is building evaluations and sometimes model organisms, where we deliberately try to produce or elicit behaviours that we really don't want in the wild. Some of that is dual use in a fairly direct way. If our methods or our results got out before we'd thought carefully about them, that could be bad, and not just for us.

And then the third, which I think people underrate, is that the threat model gets worse over time. Right now the main concern is probably humans: state actors, or people who want model weights or want to know what's going on inside labs. But if you take our own research seriously, then at some point the thing you're evaluating might itself be an adversary. If you're running a model in your infrastructure and you're trying to figure out whether it's scheming, you'd better be fairly confident it can't exfiltrate itself, tamper with your evals, or quietly change what you're measuring. That's a different kind of security problem, and I think most organisations, including us, are early on it.

I'd also just say, on a more cultural level, that taking security seriously signals that you're a serious organisation. A lot of AI safety work started in a fairly academic, open, everyone-shares-everything mode, which is great in many ways. But as the stakes have gone up, I think it's right that we've had to become more like a company that handles genuinely sensitive material. It's less fun in some ways. It costs real time and money. But I think it's one of those things where if you get it wrong once, you may not get a second chance.

astra-6.text:
For us, internal security is important because we might end up handling very sensitive information about AI systems. If we find that a model can evade oversight, for example, we want to communicate that to the people who can address it without inadvertently helping others exploit the weakness.

There’s also a trust component. If we want AI companies to give us access to their models and internal information, they need to be confident that we can protect that access. Otherwise, we might not get to do the evaluations that are most useful.

And I think it’s worth building those habits early. You don’t want to wait until you have a particularly consequential finding to start thinking about who can access it and how you keep it secure.

sol-6.1.text:
We’re trying to find out whether advanced AI systems can deceive their developers and hide dangerous capabilities. That means we might end up with quite sensitive information: evidence of a vulnerability, for example, or results that affect whether a model should be deployed. We need to be able to protect that information and share it responsibly.

There’s also the integrity of the research itself. If someone could access our evaluations or tamper with our results, that could undermine the conclusions we draw. And as the systems we evaluate become more capable, we have to consider the possibility that a model itself might try to interfere with an evaluation.

So internal security is part of making our research trustworthy. If we want labs and other partners to give us access to sensitive systems, they need confidence that we can handle that access responsibly.
